claims.claim: An ecosystem is a community of living (biotic) organisms interacting with one another and with the non-living (abiotic) environment in a defined area, connected by one-way energy flow and the cycling of matter/nutrients.

The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) classifies ecosystem services into four categories: provisioning (e.g., food, fresh water), regulating (e.g., water purification), cultural (e.g., recreation, aesthetics), and supporting (e.g., soil formation), and this remains the most widely used framework.

The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment was a four-year study (2001-2005) involving over 1,300 scientists, and found that approximately 60% (15 of 24) of the ecosystem services it examined are being degraded or used unsustainably.
Natural capital is the stock of renewable and non-renewable natural resources that yields a flow of benefits (ecosystem services) to people; the stock-versus-flow distinction is central.

Renewable resources are replenished by natural processes on a human timescale but can still be depleted if overused; non-renewable resources (minerals, fossil fuels) form over geologic time and do not replenish within human lifespans; groundwater is intermediate because recharge is often much slower than withdrawal.

Biodiversity is critical to ecosystem stability and function: species-rich communities are healthier and more productive than depleted ones, and productive ecosystems cannot be sustained without maintaining biodiversity.
Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum population size an environment can sustain given available resources; it is the equilibrium term in the logistic growth model.

In 'The Tragedy of the Commons' (Science, 1968), Garrett Hardin argued that users of an open-access shared resource tend to overuse it because each gains the full benefit of additional use while the costs of degradation are shared among all users, leading to collective ruin absent private property or state control.

Elinor Ostrom received the 2009 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 'for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons,' documenting that communities can govern shared resources sustainably through self-crafted rules, so collapse is not inevitable.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether shared common-pool resources inevitably lead to overuse and collapse.
positions: Hardin (1968): unmanaged open-access resources tend toward overuse and ruin; solutions are private property or government regulation.
Ostrom (1990, Nobel 2009): empirical case studies show many communities sustainably self-govern common-pool resources without privatization or central control.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as complementary rather than contradictory: Hardin identifies the failure mode of unmanaged open access, while Ostrom identifies the institutional conditions (clear boundaries, locally matched rules, monitoring, enforcement, conflict resolution) under which users avoid it. The lesson attributes both and adjudicates neither as universally correct.

sourceRecords.title: More Information on Ecosystem Services and EnviroAtlas
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports the definition of ecosystem services and the four-category framework (provisioning: food and fresh water; regulating: water purification; cultural: recreation and aesthetics; supporting: soil formation), which the page explicitly attributes to the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment as 'the most widely used ecosystem services framework.' Also supports that biodiversity functions as the foundation for ecosystem services rather than as a service itself. U.S. federal work; treated as reference-only and reworded originally.

sourceRecords.title: Ecosystems and Human Well-being: Synthesis (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment)
sourceRecords.notes: The canonical 2005 MA Synthesis (the primary source for the four ecosystem-service categories and the degradation finding). The full PDF exceeded the fetcher's size limit, so the framework was confirmed via the EPA EnviroAtlas page (which attributes the four categories to the MA by name) and the FAO MA summary page (read via WebFetch 2026-08-19), which confirms the assessment took four years (2001-2005) and involved over 1,300 (FAO: 1,365) experts. The headline finding that approximately 60% of examined ecosystem services (15 of 24) are being degraded or used unsustainably is the MA's widely reported conclusion. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Biodiversity Critical to Maintaining Healthy Ecosystems
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports that biodiversity is critical to the stability and productivity of ecosystems: 'you cannot have sustainable, productive ecosystems without maintaining biodiversity in the landscape' and that species-rich communities are 'substantially healthier and more productive than those depleted of species.' Also lists biodiversity-supported benefits (oxygen production, soil formation, water detoxification) and the point that reduced diversity lowers ecosystems' capacity to respond to stress. U.S. federal work; reworded originally.

sourceRecords.title: Sustainability of Ground-Water Resources (USGS Circular 1186)
sourceRecords.notes: Identified via WebSearch on 2026-08-19 (USGS Circular 1186). Supports the renewable/non-renewable distinction and the intermediate status of groundwater: it is neither non-renewable like a petroleum deposit nor completely renewable like solar energy, because recharge from precipitation replenishes it but often at much smaller rates than withdrawals. Also supports that metallic and non-metallic mineral resources are normally considered non-renewable. U.S. federal work; reworded originally.

sourceRecords.title: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2009 (Elinor Ostrom)
sourceRecords.notes: Confirmed via WebSearch of NobelPrize.org on 2026-08-19 (the /facts/ subpage returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; the canonical summary page URL is recorded). Supports that Elinor Ostrom was awarded the 2009 prize 'for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons,' shared with Oliver E. Williamson, and that she was the first woman to receive the economics prize. Her work documented community self-governance of common-pool resources (Swiss pastures, Philippine irrigation, Maine lobster fisheries). No wording reproduced beyond the short official citation, quoted with attribution.

sourceRecords.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
sourceRecords.provider: Garrett Hardin, Science, vol. 162, no. 3859, pp. 1243-1248 (13 Dec 1968)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the tragedy-of-the-commons argument, identified via WebSearch on 2026-08-19 (DOI 10.1126/science.162.3859.1243; based on Hardin's 25 June 1968 AAAS Pacific Division presidential address, published 13 Dec 1968). Supports the herdsman/pasture reasoning that each user gains the full benefit of added use while the cost of overuse is shared, so open-access resources tend toward collective overuse, and Hardin's proposed remedies of private property or government regulation. Copyrighted Science article; REFERENCE_ONLY, no text reproduced, argument summarized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Natural Capital and Ecosystem Services FAQ
sourceRecords.provider: United Nations System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch on 2026-08-19. Supports the definition of natural capital as 'the stock of renewable and non-renewable resources (e.g. plants, animals, air, water, soils, minerals) that combine to yield a flow of benefits to people' and the key stock-versus-flow distinction, with ecosystem services described as 'the contributions of ecosystems to benefits used in economic and other human activity.' Intergovernmental source; reworded originally.
